title: Early Islamic Preservation: Companions to Codification
subtitle: How hadith were transmitted and tested without treating every report as certain
summary: Hadith preservation is not the same claim as Quranic preservation. Individual reports passed through oral teaching and writing and were evaluated through chains, narrator criticism, and comparison of wording. This gives strong reports a serious evidential basis, while leaving fabrication, shared sources, hidden defects, and disagreements as questions to investigate rather than deny.

seo.metaTitle: Early Islamic Hadith Preservation: Transmission, Authentication, Codification
seo.metaDescription: How writing, named chains, and wording comparison support strong hadith, while fabrication and shared sources require critical judgment.

sections.title: The Quran and Hadith Require Different Questions
sections.body:
The Quran is a publicly received scripture with an early written standard. A hadith is a report about Muhammad's words, actions, or approval. Its authority depends on authentication and interpretation, not simply on someone attaching his name.

The central Muslim defense of hadith is therefore a critical one: reports can be compared, transmitters examined, and false attribution rejected. That is a stronger claim than saying every traditional story is certain.

sections.title: Writing Did Not Begin With the Famous Collections
sections.body:
[Bukhari 113](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:113) preserves Abu Hurayra's comparison with Abdullah ibn Amr, who wrote reports. [Muslim 3004](https://sunnah.com/muslim:3004) preserves a prohibition on writing material other than the Quran. These reports show why a simple 'all written' or 'none written' story fails.

Muslim scholars discuss their scope and possible sequence. One should not turn a proposed reconciliation into a directly witnessed fact. The safest broad account is an early mixture of memory, notes, and teaching, followed by increasingly organized collections.

sections.title: What a Chain Contributes
sections.body:
An isnad names the people through whom a report is said to have passed. This gives an attribution an inspectable structure: who learned from whom, whether contact was possible, and how the report changes among students.

A chain is valuable information, not a certificate that authenticates itself. It can contain a mistaken attribution, an unnoticed gap, or a deliberate fabrication. Muslim critics developed methods precisely because the presence of names was not enough.

sections.title: Why Comparing Versions Matters
sections.body:
Narrator criticism asks about reliability and precision; comparison asks whether a report's versions support or undermine one another. Multiple chains count for more when they are genuinely separate, not merely later branches of a shared source.

An apparent contradiction can expose an error, but it may also concern different occasions or imprecise wording. The work is to establish which explanation fits the evidence, not to label anything convenient authentic and anything difficult fabricated. [Muslim's introduction](https://sunnah.com/muslim/introduction) gives primary evidence for the critical concerns of a major compiler.

sections.title: The Book's Date Is Not Every Report's Date
sections.body:
The best-known Sunni collections of Bukhari and Muslim were compiled in the ninth century. Earlier collections, such as Malik's Muwatta, and earlier transmitted material precede them. A compilation date therefore does not show that every report was invented at that date.

The reverse also matters: a compiler's claim to an early source does not prove it. Dating an individual report requires studying its routes, wording, and earlier attestations. A modern printed book's title is not a substitute for that work.

sections.title: Why an Automatic Victory Over the Gospels Fails
sections.body:
Hadith foreground named chains and grades; Gospel study foregrounds authorial testimony, sources, manuscript relationships, and early reception. Both traditions used oral teaching and written material.

A named chain is not automatically better than every anonymous source. Nor does a Gospel's later composition make every tradition in it late. Compare particular evidence for a particular saying rather than claiming that one institution eliminates every authenticity problem.

sections.title: The Strongest Objection: Could Chains Grow Backward?
sections.body:
A skeptic can argue that later authorities supplied earlier names or that a common source generated apparently independent routes. That is a serious objection because fabricated transmission did occur.

The answer is not an assumption that Muslim critics could never be fooled. It is case-by-case comparison: divergent routes and wordings can sometimes reveal an earlier core or expose later additions. Traditional and modern scholars disagree about how far this succeeds. Strong convergence supports confidence; weak or dependent evidence should remain weak.

sections.title: Grades Protect Rather Than Diminish the Sunnah
sections.body:
Sahih means a report meets a scholar's authenticity criteria; it does not mean every reader has equal certainty about every historical detail or its legal application. Scholars can differ over a narrator, a hidden defect, or the interpretation of a sound text.

Quran 33:21 explains why believers care about Muhammad's example, and 3:31 connects following him with love of God. Those verses establish the importance of the Sunnah within Islam; they do not authenticate each individual narration.

sections.title: Why Strong Reports Deserve Serious Attention
sections.body:
The positive case for authenticated hadith is neither blind trust nor the claim that late collection destroys all memory. It is the convergence of identifiable transmission, comparison, earlier material where available, and public practice. These can provide substantial grounds for particular reports.

Religious authority and historical confidence still need to be stated at the right level. A disputed report cannot carry an argument as though every Muslim scholar—or every historian—agreed on it.

sections.title: A Better Question Than 'Are All Hadith Reliable?'
sections.body:
Ask instead: which report, which version, which grading, and what evidence supports it? Then ask what the wording actually means in context.

Use this method when reading [Who Is Prophet Muhammad?](/articles/who-is-prophet-muhammad). It lets character evidence contribute to the case while preventing attractive stories, hostile rumors, or isolated screenshots from deciding it.

bibleVerses.text: The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.
For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,

Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” Amen.
Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness,

For there are three who testify:
the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and the three agree as one.

Everyone went to his own house,
but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives.
Now very early in the morning, he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him. He sat down, and taught them.
The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman taken in adultery. Having set her in the middle,
they told him, “Teacher, we found this woman in adultery, in the very act.
Now in our law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. What then do you say about her?”
They said this testing him, that they might have something to accuse him of.
But Jesus stooped down, and wrote on the ground with his finger.
But when they continued asking him, he looked up and said to them,
“He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.”

Again he stooped down, and with his finger wrote on the ground.
They, when they heard it, being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last. Jesus was left alone with the woman where she was, in the middle.
Jesus, standing up, saw her and said,
“Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you?”
She said, “No one, Lord.”
Jesus said,
“Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.”

Now when he had risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. When they heard that he was alive, and had been seen by her, they disbelieved. After these things he was revealed in another form to two of them, as they walked, on their way into the country. They went away and told it to the rest. They didn’t believe them, either. Afterward he was revealed to the eleven themselves as they sat at the table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they didn’t believe those who had seen him after he had risen. He said to them, “Go into all the world, and preach the Good News to the whole creation. He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who disbelieves will be condemned. These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak with new languages; they will take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it will in no way hurt them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover.” So then the Lord, after he had spoken to them, was received up into heaven, and sat down at the right hand of God. They went out, and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them, and confirming the word by the signs that followed. Amen.
I solemnly command you by the Lord that this letter be read to all the holy brothers.

faq.question: Are hadith the same as the Quran?
faq.answer: No. The Quran is Islam's primary scripture. Hadith are reports about the messenger, individually assessed for authenticity and interpreted alongside the Quran and the wider Sunnah.

faq.question: Were no hadith written before Bukhari?
faq.answer: That is incorrect. Earlier collections and reports of early writing exist. Their existence does not automatically authenticate every later narration.

faq.question: Does sahih mean nobody can question a report?
faq.answer: No. It is an authenticity judgment under defined criteria. Scholars can debate particular narrations and their meaning without treating all reports as equally uncertain.

faq.question: Do several chains always mean independent confirmation?
faq.answer: No. Chains can branch from a shared source or have hidden dependence. Their relationships must be examined along with wording.

faq.question: What should a beginner do with a disturbing hadith?
faq.answer: Find the exact source and wording, check its grading and relevant variants, and seek a qualified explanation that addresses the real moral question. Do not assume that an unattributed translation or a single screenshot settles it.

furtherReading.title: Sahih Muslim, Introduction
furtherReading.author: Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj
furtherReading.note: A major compiler's own discussion of transmission and the selection of reports; numbering differs across editions.

furtherReading.title: An Introduction to the Science of the Hadith (Kitab Ma'rifat Anwa' 'Ilm al-Hadith)
furtherReading.author: Ibn al-Salah al-Shahrazuri (13th century), translated by Eerik Dickinson
furtherReading.note: A foundational classical work on hadith authentication methodology, part of the Great Books of Islamic Civilization series, explaining jarh wa ta'dil and isnad analysis in detail.

furtherReading.title: Hadith: Muhammad's Legacy in the Medieval and Modern World
furtherReading.author: Jonathan A.C. Brown
furtherReading.note: A comprehensive academic study of hadith criticism and methodology that engages both Islamic scholarly traditions and modern Western academic perspectives, including discussion of the Goldziher-Schacht thesis and Islamic scholars' responses. Essential for understanding contemporary debates over hadith reliability.

furtherReading.title: Hadith: Origins and Developments
furtherReading.author: Edited by Harald Motzki
furtherReading.note: An edited collection of influential scholarly essays (including foundational contributions by Goldziher, Schacht, and Juynboll alongside responses) examining hadith criticism from both classical Islamic and modern Western academic perspectives, with attention to methodological issues in dating and provenance.
